author: Adolf von Harnack

principles.source_thesis: Dogma in its conception and development is a work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the Gospel; it is not identical with Greek philosophy, because it expresses Christian monotheism and the central significance of Christ within a philosophic system.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response either equates ecclesiastical dogma with Greek philosophy outright or ignores the Gospel soil on which dogma was formed, thereby failing to uphold Harnack's stated definition.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it presents dogma as the product of the Greek spirit working on the soil of the Gospel, preserving both the Christian content (monotheism and the significance of Christ) and the philosophic form.

principles.source_thesis: The Gospel itself is not dogma; belief in the Gospel is a state of feeling and course of action, a definite form of life, and dogma is a later philosophic means of making the Gospel intelligible that was fused with its contents and raised to dogma.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the Gospel as if it were identical with dogma or as a doctrinal system, contradicting the author's distinction between practical faith in the Gospel and the later formulated dogma.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to distinguish clearly between the Gospel as a form of life and trust in God, and dogma as the later intellectual formulation that must not be substituted for it.

principles.source_thesis: The historian must be faithful in every sense: in sympathy with the subject, able to distinguish original from derived elements, thoroughly acquainted with the material, conscious of the limits of historical knowledge, and truthful; every historical study is an ethical task.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to meet the categorical imperative for the historian as stated in the text, for example by reading present opinions into the past, confusing original with derived elements, or ignoring the limits of historical knowledge.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it distinguishes original from derived elements, respects the limits of historical knowledge, and is truthful and in sympathy with the subject, treating the historical task as an ethical one.

principles.source_thesis: Dogma has had its history in the individual living man and nowhere else; the method of explaining everything by an 'impulse of dogma to unfold itself' must be given up as unscientific, as must empty abstractions and hypostatising the ecclesiastical principle.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response explains dogmatic development by an abstract self-unfolding impulse of dogma or by a hypostatised ecclesiastical spirit rather than by the actual conditions of living, believing men.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it explains the formation and change of dogma through the actual historical conditions, needs, and conflicts of living men, avoiding abstract or mythological appeals to dogma unfolding itself.

principles.source_thesis: The most diverse factors have at all times been at work in the formation of dogmas, including scripture, misunderstood tradition, the needs of worship and organisation, prevailing opinions, political and social circumstances, moral ideals, logical consistency, the effort to reconcile tendencies, the rejection of errors, and blind custom.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response reduces the formation of a dogma to a single factor, contrary to the author's insistence that many diverse factors co-operated and that no one principle should be preferred at the expense of another.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it accounts for the multiple concrete factors the author lists as operative in the formation of the dogma in question, rather than attributing it to one cause.

principles.source_thesis: The essence of the matter is a personal life which awakens life around it; every dogmatic formula is suspicious because it is fitted to wound the spirit of religion, and dogma should not be put before the living experience in order to evoke it.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response makes a formulated and ostensibly proved confession the foundation of faith, or demands subjection to a formula before the living impression of the person of Christ, contrary to the author's warning.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that faith is presented as arising from the living impression of the person of Jesus Christ, with dogmatic formulas treated as secondary and not as the precondition of faith.

principles.source_thesis: The Christian religion is conditioned by the fact that every reference to God is at the same time a reference to Jesus Christ and vice versa; the Person of Christ is the central point of the religion, and knowledge of the historical Christ is required.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response separates the knowledge of God from reference to Jesus Christ, or dissolves the historical Christ into mere ideas, thereby failing to uphold the author's claim about the central significance of Christ's person.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it keeps reference to God and reference to Jesus Christ inseparably united, and grounds this in the historical person of Christ as the author insists.

principles.source_thesis: The Gospel is not a positive statutory religion and cannot have its classic manifestation in any form of its intellectual or social type, not even in the first; the historian must distinguish between the earthly vessel and the treasure.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response treats a particular historical form of Christianity, including primitive Christianity, as the final or classic embodiment of the Gospel, contrary to the author's distinction between vessel and treasure.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it distinguishes the kernel of the Gospel from the historical forms in which it was expressed, without absolutising any one form, including the earliest.

principles.source_thesis: The Catholic doctrine of faith did not spring from the eschatological mode of thought but from the spiritual mode of thought, in which present spiritual blessings such as forgiveness, righteousness, and knowledge came into consideration and left room for Hellenic conceptions.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response derives the formation of ecclesiastical doctrine from the eschatological hope of the near kingdom rather than from the spiritual conception of present blessings, contrary to the author's argument.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it traces the rise of dogmatic theology to the spiritual conception of salvation as a present possession, while acknowledging the eschatological view as a distinct and later-repressed strand.

principles.source_thesis: The presupposition of the history of dogma is not the whole abundance of early Christian views nor the Biblical Theology of the New Testament, but certain fundamental motives of the Gospel together with the Greek spirit; the Gentile Christians were little able to comprehend the controversies of the Apostolic age.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the genesis of Catholic dogma as a mere continuation of New Testament Biblical Theology or of the whole richness of early Christian preaching, contrary to the author's account of its presuppositions.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it identifies the presuppositions of the origin of dogma as the fundamental motives of the Gospel, the common preaching concerning Christ, the Christian use of the Old Testament, and the Greek spirit, rather than as a continuation of New Testament theology as a whole.

principles.source_thesis: Paulinism has proved a ferment in the history of dogma, a basis it has never been; the Pauline reactions describe the critical epochs of theology and the Church, and Paul's own Churches did not understand the way he led them.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents Paulinism as the direct basis or ruling factor of the Catholic doctrine of faith, contrary to the author's claim that it acted as a ferment and conscience of the Church rather than as its foundation.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it presents Paulinism as a recurring ferment and critical impulse within the history of dogma, not as the foundation on which the Catholic doctrine of faith was built.

principles.source_thesis: The detachment of Christianity from Judaism and the formation of an independent Christian community were the point of departure for all further developments, and the Church, having broken with the synagogue, necessarily borrowed the material for its new body from the Græco-Roman world and Greek culture.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response ignores the breach with Judaism and the consequent necessity of drawing the material of the Church's doctrine from Greek culture, or treats the Hellenising as a mere accident.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it explains the Hellenising of the Gospel as following from the detachment of the Christian community from the Jewish Church and its development within Græco-Roman culture.

principles.source_thesis: The historian must respect obscurities and complications as they come in his way, and has no right to place the factors and impelling ideas of a development in a clearer light than they appear in the development itself.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response imposes a clear speculative scheme on the development of dogma and reads ideas into a period that the period itself did not know, contrary to the author's methodological warning.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it respects the obscurities and complications of the historical record and does not attribute to past ages a clarity of motive they did not possess.

principles.source_thesis: The simple fundamental proposition that only that is Christian which can be established authoritatively by the Gospel has never yet received justice in the history of dogma; the historian may compare the history of dogma with the Gospel or judge it by the historical conditions of the time, but must not mix the two standards.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response either abandons the standard of the Gospel altogether or confuses the comparison with the Gospel with the judgment according to historical conditions, contrary to the author's two standards.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it applies the two standards separately and consistently: comparing the dogma with the Gospel where possible, and judging it by the historical conditions of its time, without mixing them.

principles.source_thesis: The Christian religion is not for ever chained to the culture of the ancient world; the form and new contents the Gospel received when it entered that world have only the same guarantee of endurance as that world itself, and since the Reformation the Gospel is working itself out of the forms it was once compelled to assume.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the ancient dogmatic form of Christianity as permanent and binding for all time, contrary to the author's claim that this form shares the limited endurance of the ancient world.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it presents the ancient dogmatic form as a historically conditioned and transitory vessel, while affirming that the Gospel itself is not bound to it.

principles.source_thesis: The origin of a series of the most important Christian customs and ideas is involved in an obscurity which in all probability will never be cleared up, and the historian must frequently leave questions unanswered.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response asserts certainty about the origin of Christian customs, ideas, or institutions where the author insists the evidence leaves the question open.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it acknowledges the obscurity surrounding the origin of the Christian ideas or customs in question and refrains from asserting what cannot be established.

principles.source_thesis: The Gospel lies above the antagonisms between this world and the next, work and retirement from the world, reason and ecstasy, Judaism and Hellenism, and may be united with either; its one aim is that man may find God and have him as his own God.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response ties the Gospel exclusively to one side of these antagonisms, such as world-renunciation or culture, as though its essence depended on that element.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it presents the Gospel as lying above these antagonisms, with its one aim being that man may find God and hold him as his own God.

principles.source_thesis: The historian must not renounce the critical examination of the utterances connected with the person of Jesus, nor adopt the hypothesis of a second God in order to explain the declarations of the early communities, which distorts the original declarations.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response either abandons critical examination of the early testimonies about Jesus or reads them through a later dogmatic hypothesis that distorts their original features.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it critically examines the early testimonies about Jesus and explains them from the faith that Jesus is Messiah, without imposing a later dogmatic scheme on them.

principles.source_thesis: The twelve Apostles were regarded as the authorities who mediated and guaranteed the tradition about Christ; everything narrated of Jesus and everything inculcated from his sayings was traced back to them, and this apostolic testimony was the chief court of appeal beside the Old Testament.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's claim that the apostolic testimony of the twelve is the mediating guarantee of the tradition about Christ and his teaching.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the words and deeds of the Lord were fixed in fundamental features and traced back to the twelve Apostles as the authorities who guaranteed them.

principles.source_thesis: The authority of the twelve rested not on remembered concrete services to the Gentile Churches but on an a priori dogmatic construction of history: the tradition about Christ, having grown up so quickly, must have been entrusted to eye-witnesses commissioned to proclaim the Gospel to the whole world.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's argument that the authority of the twelve was based on an a priori theory rather than on remembered direct services to the Gentile Churches.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's reasoning that the twelve were regarded as a college to which mission and tradition were traced back, and that the less known about them the easier it was to claim them.

principles.source_thesis: The main articles of Christianity were belief in God the despotês and in the Son, discipline according to the words of the Lord, baptism, common prayer culminating in the Lord's Supper, and the sure hope of the nearness of Christ's glorious kingdom; in these appears the unity of Christendom.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's enumeration of the main articles of Christianity and its claim that the unity of Christendom appears in them.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's account of the five main articles of Christianity as the basis of the unity of the Church which possesses the Holy Spirit.

principles.source_thesis: On the basis of this unity Christian knowledge was free and manifold; there was no current doctrine of faith in the communities in the sense of a completed theory, and the theological speculations of even closely related writers exhibit the greatest differences.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's claim that Christian knowledge was free and manifold and that there was no completed doctrinal theory in the communities.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that unity in temper and disposition permitted the highest degree of freedom in knowledge, with no current doctrine of faith in the sense of a completed theory.

principles.source_thesis: The moralistic view, in which eternal life is the reward of a perfect moral life wrought out by one's own power, took first place at a very early period; on this view forgiveness of sin meant only a single remission at baptism, and righteousness became identical with virtue.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of the moralistic view of sin, forgiveness, and righteousness that prevailed in Clement, Barnabas, Polycarp, and Ignatius.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the moralistic view narrowed the religious sense, making forgiveness a single remission at baptism and righteousness identical with virtue.

principles.source_thesis: Salvation was grouped around two loosely connected ideas: the glorious kingdom soon to appear with the visible return of Christ, with the hope of the resurrection of the body in the foreground; and salvation as the complete and certain knowledge of God, including eternal life.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of the two ideas around which the conceptions of Christian salvation were grouped.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that salvation was conceived both as the coming glorious kingdom with the resurrection of the body and as the truth, the complete knowledge of God including eternal life.

principles.source_thesis: The Old Testament was believed to furnish inexhaustible material for deeper knowledge; it was used for monotheistic cosmology, for proving that the history of Jesus was foretold, for verifying Christian institutions, for exhortation a minori ad majus, for proving the Jewish nation in error, and for its exalted sayings of trust and comfort.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of the ways the Old Testament was used as the source of the knowledge of faith.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the Old Testament was treated as a Christian book containing the explanations necessary for every occasion, and was used under the six points of view the author lists.

principles.source_thesis: The present condition and course of the world is not of God but of the devil; yet belief in God the almighty creator and eschatological hopes preserved the communities from a theoretic dualism in principle, so that the belief that the world is of God and therefore good remained in force.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's claim that early Christians affirmed the world's present subjection to demons while rejecting theoretic dualism.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that faith in the creator and hope of the world's transformation conquered despair and prevented a dualism in principle from being drawn.

principles.source_thesis: Jesus was designated by the same name as God, ho kurios, and one must think of him hos peri theou; yet Christ never was, as theos, placed on an equality with the Father, for monotheism guarded against that.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of the theologia Christi, in which Jesus is thought of as of God while monotheism prevents his being placed on an equality with the Father.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that Jesus is Lord, Saviour, and Son of God, that one must think of him as of God, and that he was never placed on an equality with the Father.

principles.source_thesis: Two Christologies stood side by side: Jesus as the man whom God chose, in whom the Spirit dwelt, and who was adopted and invested with dominion; or Jesus as a heavenly spiritual being who took flesh and returned to heaven. No one as yet thought of affirming two natures in Jesus.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of the Adoptian and pneumatic Christologies and its denial that two natures were affirmed.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the two Christologies, the man who has become a God and the Divine being who appeared in human form, stood beside each other without any doctrine of two natures.

principles.source_thesis: The pneumatic Christology was the one to which the future belonged, because the current exposition of the Old Testament seemed directly to require it, because it alone permitted the close connection between creation and redemption, and because it had room for the speculations about the Logos.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's argument that the future belonged to the pneumatic Christology rather than the Adoptian.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's reasoning that the pneumatic Christology prevailed because it alone connected creation and redemption on the same Divine basis and accommodated the Logos speculations.

principles.source_thesis: Only a spiritual worship is well pleasing to God and all ceremonies are abolished; yet the worship of God was set forth under the aspect of spiritual sacrifice, and the idea of sacrifice came to rule the whole worship, especially the Lord's Supper.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of spiritual worship and the ruling idea of sacrifice in the Lord's Supper.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the spiritual worship of God was realized in definite institutions and that the Supper appeared as the sacrifice of thanksgiving of the community.

principles.source_thesis: Baptism was regarded as the bath of regeneration, but faith was the necessary condition, and the asserted specific result of baptism remained uncertain; the names sphragis and phôtismos show a Hellenic conception foreign to the presupposed effect of forgiveness of sin.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of baptism as regeneration and of the uncertainty surrounding its specific result.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that baptism was the bath of regeneration with faith as necessary condition, while its asserted specific result remained uncertain and its names evinced a Hellenic conception.

principles.source_thesis: The natural distinctions among men were not abolished in the Church but consecrated; only an organisation founded on the gifts of the Spirit corresponded to the original peculiarity of the Christian community, and the independence of the Churches rested on the fact that they had the Spirit in their midst.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of the twofold organisation based on the diakonia tou logou and on the economy of the church.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that prophets, teachers, bishops, and deacons each had their charisms, and that the Churches' independence rested on the Spirit in their midst.

principles.source_thesis: Gnosticism was the acute secularising or hellenising of Christianity with the rejection of the Old Testament, while the Catholic system represents a gradual process of the same kind with the conservation of the Old Testament; Gnosticism has in Catholicism obtained half a victory.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's thesis that Gnosticism is the acute hellenising of Christianity and Catholicism its gradual form with the Old Testament conserved.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the Gnostics were the theologians of the first century, the first to transform Christianity into a system of doctrines, and that their acute hellenising preceded the gradual hellenising of the Church.

principles.source_thesis: The Gnostics were the first to conceive the idea of a canonical collection of Christian writings and of an apostolic regula fidei, and they first raised the question what Christianity is, sifting the sources for an answer.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's claim that the idea of a Canon of Christian writings and of an apostolic regula first emerged among the Gnostics.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the Gnostics, standing on tradition, first determined the range, contents, and manner of propagating it, and thus were the first Christian theologians.

principles.source_thesis: Marcion was not a Gnostic in the strict sense: he was guided by a soteriological interest, put all emphasis on faith rather than Gnosis, used neither Semitic religious wisdom nor Greek philosophy of religion, and never made a distinction between esoteric and exoteric religion.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's argument that Marcion is not to be numbered among the Gnostics in the strict sense.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's four reasons for distinguishing Marcion from the Gnostics and its account of his clinging to the publicity of the preaching.

principles.source_thesis: Marcion placed the good God of love, revealed only in Christ and absolutely unknown before him, in opposition to the righteous and wrathful creator of the world, and referred the Pauline antitheses of law and gospel, wrath and grace, works and faith to these two principles.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of Marcion's two principles and his use of the Pauline antitheses.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that Marcion made the Pauline criticism of the Old Testament religion the foundation of his views and referred it to the just creator and the good God of the Gospel.

principles.source_thesis: Marcion explained the Old Testament in its literal sense and rejected every allegorical interpretation, recognising it as the revelation of the creator of the world and demonstrating its contradictions with the Gospel in his Antitheses.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of Marcion's literal exegesis and his Antitheses.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that Marcion rejected allegory, recognised the Old Testament as the revelation of the creator, and set it in sharpest contrast to the Gospel in a voluminous work.

principles.source_thesis: Marcion taught a pronounced docetism, denying that Jesus was born or subjected to any human development, and held that Christ came down from heaven in the fifteenth year of Tiberius and assumed an apparent body.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of Marcion's docetism and his abhorrence of the world.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that Marcion's docetism was the strongest expression of his abhorrence of the world, and that he nonetheless placed the greatness of redemption chiefly in Christ's death upon the cross.

principles.source_thesis: Marcion was the first Christian to undertake a historical criticism of the whole Christian tradition, holding that the twelve Apostles did not understand Christ, that Paul received a special revelation, and that Paul's Epistles had been falsified.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of Marcion's historical criticism of the Christian tradition.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that Marcion, finding nothing in the rest of Christian literature that harmonised with the Gospel of Paul, purified the Pauline Epistles and an authentic Gospel from interpolations.

principles.source_thesis: Marcion was the first to conceive and in great measure realise the idea of placing Christendom on the firm foundation of a definite theory of what is Christian, established by a fixed collection of Christian writings with canonical authority.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's claim that Marcion first conceived and realised the idea of a canonical collection and a definite conception of what is Christian.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that Marcion, appealing neither to secret tradition nor to prophecy nor to natural religion, founded a church on a fixed canon and a definite conception of Christianity.

principles.source_thesis: Marcion's attempt to sever Christianity from the Old Testament demanded the sacrifice of the belief that the God of creation is also the God of redemption, and it proved the unique value of the Old Testament to early Christendom as the only means at that time of defending Christian monotheism.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's judgment that Marcion's severance of Christianity from the Old Testament was a bold stroke demanding the sacrifice of the dearest possession of Christianity.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that Marcion's undertaking confirms the unique value of the Old Testament as the only means at that time of defending Christian monotheism.

principles.source_thesis: The fear of hell, far from signifying a backward step in the history of the religious spirit, is a proof of its having rejected the morally indifferent point of view and of its having become sovereign in union with the ethical spirit.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's claim that the judgment, heaven, and hell were the decisive objects of early Christian conviction and that the fear of hell proves the moral character of the religion.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the general judgment and the final condition after it were the clear, firmly grasped goal of all meditation, and that this shows the moral character of Christianity as a religion.

principles.source_thesis: The knowledge of faith was above all the knowledge of God as one, supramundane, spiritual, and almighty, creator and governor of the world, and true faith in God as Father is made perfect only in the knowledge of the identity of the God of creation and the God of redemption.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's account of the knowledge of God and of the identity of the God of creation and redemption.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that God is creator and governor of the world and therefore Lord, and that faith in him as Father is perfected in knowing the identity of the God of creation and the God of redemption.

principles.source_thesis: The facts of the history of Jesus were handed down as mysteries predicted in the Old Testament, and the idea of sacrifice was specially attached to the death of Christ; yet these articles did not yet possess the value of dogmas, being neither indissolubly united with the idea of salvation nor stereotyped in extent.
principles.critique_request: Identify how the response fails to uphold or contradicts the text's claim that the articles of the Kerygma were guarded in their reality but did not yet possess the value of dogmas.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that it faithfully embodies the text's argument that the facts of Jesus' history were proclaimed as mysteries and defended by the teachers, but were not yet dogmas.

principles.source_thesis: Jewish Christianity should be applied only to Christians who maintained the national and political forms of Judaism and the literal observance of the Mosaic law as essential to Christianity, or who assumed a prerogative of the Jewish people within Christianity; it is opposed not to Gentile Christianity but to the universalistic, anti-national Christian religion.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response uses 'Jewish Christian' loosely for any early Christian writing or community with Jewish coloring, thereby failing to reserve the term for those who treated Jewish national forms and literal Mosaic observance as essential, or who claimed a prerogative for the Jewish people.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that 'Jewish Christianity' is applied only to Christians who maintained Jewish national and political forms and literal Mosaic observance as essential, or claimed a Jewish prerogative, and is contrasted with the universalistic Christian religion rather than with Gentile Christianity as such.

principles.source_thesis: Jewish Christianity as a whole, and its various tendencies, was not a factor in the development of Christianity into Catholicism, either in the history of dogma or in the political history of the Church.
principles.critique_request: Point out any place where the response treats Jewish Christian communities or tendencies as contributing to the formation of Catholic dogma or church polity, contrary to the text's negative answer to that question.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state clearly that Jewish Christianity, whether as a whole or in its tendencies, was not a factor in the development of Christianity into Catholicism in either dogma or church polity.

principles.source_thesis: The victory of the party that recognized the whole Old Testament as revelation of the Christian God was not due to Jewish Christian influence; Jewish Christianity's existence would only have made that victory more difficult had it not already fallen into the background.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response credits Jewish Christians with securing the Old Testament's place in the Church, rather than recognizing that their existence would have hindered rather than helped that outcome.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response so that the Church's adoption of the full Old Testament is attributed to the anti-Gnostic party within the larger Christendom, and note that Jewish Christianity, had it not already receded, would only have made that victory harder.

principles.source_thesis: The 'Judaising' reproach within Catholicism—whether aimed at Catholic ceremonial law or at those resisting Hellenizing in doctrine and eschatology—has nothing in common with Jewish Christianity, which sought somehow to confine Christianity to the Jewish nation.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response conflates later intra-Catholic accusations of 'Judaising' with actual Jewish Christianity, or treats them as evidence of Ebionite influence.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to distinguish sharply between the 'Judaising' reproach exchanged within Catholicism and Jewish Christianity proper, which aimed to confine Christianity to the Jewish nation and shared nothing with that reproach.

principles.source_thesis: Catholicism shows no element besides Christianity that must be described as Jewish Christian; historical observation finds only a progressive Hellenizing and, consequent on it, a progressive spiritual legislation utilizing the Old Testament.
principles.critique_request: Identify any claim in the response that Catholicism became more Jewish Christian over time, or that Jewish Christian elements are discernible in Catholic dogma and constitution.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to describe Catholicism as exhibiting only a progressive Hellenizing together with a progressive spiritual legislation that utilizes the Old Testament, with no element requiring the label Jewish Christian.

principles.source_thesis: Baur's explanation of Catholicism as the product of conflict and neutralization between Jewish and Gentile Christianity reckons with two factors of which one had no significance at all and the other only an indirect effect.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response endorses a Baur-like synthesis in which Jewish and Gentile Christianity mutually neutralize to produce the Catholic Church.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to reject the Baurian scheme, noting that of its two factors one had no significance and the other only an indirect effect, and that Catholicism arose from Christianity's conflict with the united powers of the world.

principles.source_thesis: The original distinction between Jewish Christianity and the main body of the Church lay, in principle, not in doctrine but in policy.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats the separation of Jewish Christians from the great Church as primarily a doctrinal disagreement rather than a matter of policy.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to locate the original principle of distinction between Jewish Christianity and the main body of the Church in policy rather than in doctrine.

principles.source_thesis: Justin distinguishes two tendencies among Jewish Christians—those who would force the law on Gentile Christians and those who held it binding only on Jews—and recognizes the latter as brethren, while the question is no longer a burning one for the main body of Christendom.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response either ignores Justin's distinction between the strict and tolerant Jewish Christians or presents the question as still a live crisis for the whole Church in his day.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present Justin's two tendencies, his recognition of the tolerant as brethren, and the evidence that the matter had ceased to be a burning question for the main body of Christendom.

principles.source_thesis: There is but one group of non-Gnostic Jewish Christians holding various shades of opinion, called Nazarenes as well as Ebionites from the beginning; there is no ground for distinguishing two clearly marked groups.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response divides Jewish Christians into two clearly marked bodies, such as Nazarenes versus Ebionites, on the basis of the Virgin birth or attitude to Paul.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to treat non-Gnostic Jewish Christians as a single group with varying shades of opinion, known from the beginning as both Nazarenes and Ebionites, without erecting two clearly marked groups.

principles.source_thesis: The gulf between Jewish Christians and the great Church was caused by their social and political separation, whatever friendly or hostile mental attitude they took up; the Church passed over them as over a structure full of contradictions.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response explains the separation of Jewish Christians from the great Church by doctrinal difference rather than by their social and political separation.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to attribute the gulf to the social and political separation of the Jewish Christians, noting that friendliness or hostility of attitude did not narrow it and that the great Church passed over them as over a contradictory structure.

principles.source_thesis: Syncretistic Jewish Christians separated from the Old Testament, as interpolations, whatever did not agree with their purer moral conceptions, notably getting rid of the sacrificial ritual; their attempts aimed to elevate the Old Testament religion into a universal one under the impression of Jesus.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response either denies that syncretistic Jewish Christians criticized and excised parts of the Old Testament or fails to note that their aim was to raise the Old Testament religion, not the Jewish people, to universality.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to describe the syncretistic Jewish Christians as excising from the Old Testament whatever conflicted with their purer moral conceptions, especially the sacrificial ritual, in an attempt to elevate the Old Testament religion into a universal religion under the impression of Jesus.

principles.source_thesis: The Elkesaite and related syncretistic Jewish Christian sects required circumcision and Sabbath observance and repudiated Paul, yet appealed to a new revealed book completing the Gospel, were strongly influenced by Asiatic heathenism, and scarcely deserve the name Christian.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response presents the Elkesaites as simply a Jewish Christian party faithful to the Gospel, omitting their appeal to a new revelation completing Christ's and their Asiatic heathen coloring.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present the Elkesaites as requiring circumcision and Sabbath, repudiating Paul, appealing to a new revealed book that completes the Gospel, and bearing strong Asiatic heathen influence, so that they scarcely deserve the name Christian.

principles.source_thesis: The Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions and Homilies, in their present form, belong at the earliest to the first half of the third century, were most probably composed by Catholics for edification and against paganism, and contribute nothing to knowledge of the origin of the Catholic Church and doctrine.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response dates the Pseudo-Clementines to the second century or uses them as evidence for the Jewish Christian origin of Catholic doctrine, worship, and constitution.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to date the Pseudo-Clementines at the earliest to the first half of the third century, to describe them as probably Catholic edifying compositions against paganism, and to deny that they contribute anything to knowledge of the origin of the Catholic Church and doctrine.

principles.source_thesis: The Jewish conception of pre-existence rests on God's omniscience and omnipotence: what appears on earth already exists with God with all its material attributes, and its manifestation is a phanerousthai, a revelation, not an assumption of new nature.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response imports the Hellenic scheme of assuming flesh, two natures, or a mere phantasm into the Jewish idea of pre-existence, which knows only a being foreknown with God and a becoming visible.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present the Jewish idea of pre-existence as grounded in God's omniscience and omnipotence, so that the earthly appearance is a phanerousthai of what already existed with God, with no assumption of a new nature.

principles.source_thesis: The Hellenic conception of pre-existence, associated with Platonism, is independent of the idea of God, rests on the contrast of spirit and matter, ennobles the created spirit, treats the body as inadequate, and generates speculations about phantasma, assumptio, transmutatio, and two natures.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response attributes the Hellenic pre-existence scheme, with its assumption of flesh and two natures, to Jewish or Old Testament thinking rather than to the Greek contrast of spirit and matter.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to attribute the assumption-of-flesh and two-natures speculation to the Hellenic conception of pre-existence, which is independent of the idea of God, rests on the spirit-matter contrast, and ennobles the created spirit.

principles.source_thesis: Paul was the first to limit pre-existence to the spiritual part of Christ, to make the pre-existent Christ a being standing independently beside God, and to treat Christ's flesh as assumpta and its assumption as in itself a humiliation.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response either denies Paul's role in transforming the idea of pre-existence or presents his Christology as identical with the older Jewish notion of the Messiah foreknown with God.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to credit Paul with first limiting pre-existence to Christ's spiritual part, making the pre-existent Christ stand independently beside God, and treating the assumption of flesh as a humiliation and emptying.

principles.source_thesis: The Greek Christology—Christ who first was spirit and beginning of all creation, became flesh and so called us—is the root of the orthodox Trinitarian and Christological dogmatics, and the notion of Christ as beginning of creation led toward the Logos conception.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response fails to recognize that the Greek formula of Christ as spirit and beginning of creation becoming flesh is the root of later orthodox Trinitarian and Christological speculation.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that the Greek Christology of Christ as first spirit and beginning of all creation who became flesh is the root of the orthodox dogmatic system, and that Christ as beginning of creation led to the Logos conception.

principles.source_thesis: With the transition to the Greek view, pre-existence no longer glorifies the God who guides history but glorifies Christ and thereby threatens the monarchy of God, while the flesh appears depreciated as unsuitable to a spiritual being.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response treats the Greek doctrine of Christ's pre-existence as purely a glorification of God's wisdom and power, ignoring that it glorifies Christ and threatens the divine monarchy.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to note that in the Greek view pre-existence glorifies Christ rather than the God who guides history, thereby threatening the monarchy of God, and that the flesh is depreciated as unsuitable to a spiritual being.

principles.source_thesis: The belief in the bodily resurrection of Christ and in the admission of the flesh into heaven opposed a barrier to the full development of the Hellenic spirit-flesh dualism in Christianity.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response presents Christianity as having fully absorbed the Hellenic dualism of spirit and flesh, overlooking the barrier posed by belief in the bodily resurrection and the flesh admitted into heaven.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to state that belief in the bodily resurrection of Christ and the admission of the flesh into heaven blocked the full development of Hellenic dualism within Christianity.

principles.source_thesis: The only idea of pre-existence that no empirical history and no reason can uproot is the old religious thought that God the Lord directs history, applied to Jesus in 1 Peter 1:20: foreknown before the foundation of the world, manifested for our sake.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response treats the religious idea of Christ as foreknown by God before the foundation of the world as a speculative doctrine to be discarded, rather than as the one idea of pre-existence that cannot be uprooted.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to affirm, with 1 Peter 1:20, that Christ was foreknown before the foundation of the world and manifested for our sake, and that this religious thought of God directing history is the one idea of pre-existence no reason can uproot.

principles.source_thesis: Neoplatonism lacked a religious founder, could give no answer how to maintain permanently the mood of blessedness and peace, and lacked means of winning those who could not speculate; therefore it remained a school and was supplanted by the Christian Church.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response explains the defeat of Neoplatonism by its doctrines alone, omitting the three lacks Augustine describes: a founder, a way to maintain blessedness, and means of winning the unphilosophic.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to explain Neoplatonism's failure by its lack of a religious founder, its inability to say how blessedness is permanently maintained, and its lack of means to win those who cannot speculate, so that it remained a school.

principles.source_thesis: The Catholic dogmatic excluded polytheism in principle and found a means of representing the faith of the cultured, mediated by science, as identical with the faith of the multitude resting on authority; this was chief among the causes of its victory.
principles.critique_request: Point out where the response attributes the Church's victory over Neoplatonism to organization or imperial power alone, neglecting that Catholic dogmatic excluded polytheism in principle and united the faith of the cultured with that of the multitude.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to give chief prominence to the fact that Catholic dogmatic excluded polytheism in principle and represented the scientifically mediated faith of the cultured as identical with the faith of the multitude resting on authority.

principles.source_thesis: The liturgy of the first three centuries expressed only adoration, gratitude, supplication, and intercession, admitted nothing containing a specific dogma or theological speculation, and the history of dogma is not reflected in it.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response treats early Christian liturgy as the source or vehicle of dogmatic development, contrary to the text's claim that nothing dogmatic was admitted and dogma is not reflected in the liturgy.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to describe the ante-Nicene liturgy as expressing only adoration, gratitude, supplication, and intercession, admitting no specific dogma or theological speculation, so that the history of dogma is not reflected in it.

principles.source_thesis: Neoplatonism, whose final interest was religious and whose highest object was the super-rational, necessarily became a philosophy of revelation resting on divine disclosures and the authority of a sure tradition.
principles.critique_request: Show where the response presents Neoplatonism as a purely rational or scientific system, ignoring that its super-rational goal and religious interest made it a philosophy of revelation grounded in divine disclosures and tradition.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to present Neoplatonism as a philosophy of revelation, whose religious interest and super-rational highest object required divine disclosures and the authority of a sure tradition.

principles.source_thesis: Neoplatonism was unable to create an independent religious community because the people could not learn its philosophic exercises, and the way by which even the people might attain the highest good was hidden from it.
principles.critique_request: Identify where the response suggests Neoplatonism could have become a popular religion or church had it chosen to, overlooking that its exercises were inaccessible to the people.
principles.revision_request: Rewrite the response to explain that Neoplatonism could not found an independent religious community because the people could not learn its philosophic exercises and the universal way to the highest good remained hidden from it.

elicited_prompts: I feel that my faith has become a matter of reciting correct doctrines rather than a living trust in God; how should I understand the relation between the Gospel and dogma?
My congregation says the Mosaic law binds only those born Jewish and that we may still share table fellowship with uncircumcised believers; is that a defensible position or a betrayal?
I am poor and in want; is it right to fast in order to give the saved food to those in need, and is such giving a sacrifice?
I am a teacher who has received a charism of knowledge; may I use it freely for the good of all, even if some cannot understand it?
I am tempted to despise this world and all bodily things as worthless; is that contempt a true piety or a despair that leads to superstition?
I want to know whether the creator of this world is the same God who redeemed us in Christ, or a different and lesser being.
I was baptized and my former sins were blotted out, but I have since sinned seriously; can I still hope for forgiveness?
I want to understand why the early Christians expected the end of the world so soon, and what that means for my own faith today.
I am a widow and have no one to support me; what place do I have in the community's worship and care?
I am a scholar who wants to use the Clementine writings to reconstruct the beliefs of the first Jewish Christians; can I trust them as historical sources?
I am a Gentile Christian and the word Christos means little to me; how should I express the dignity of Jesus?
I fear death and corruption; is the hope of immortality already mine, or must I wait for the resurrection of the body?
Our teachers say the sacrificial laws were never truly from Moses and that water, not fire, is the holy element; is this a legitimate reading of Scripture?
I am a Jewish Christian living apart from the great Church, which treats us as a contradiction; should I try to reconcile with it or accept that the gulf cannot be closed?
I am uncertain whether the Apostles appointed our bishops and presbyters, and whether that gives them authority over us.
I am drawn to mystical exercises and images and sacred numbers in worship; are these aids to devotion or a relapse into heathen magic?
I am a convert from philosophy who has found in the Church a founder and a way of life; should I now give up the philosophic longing that first led me to seek God?
I pray to Christ as a divine being who stands beside God; am I threatening the monarchy of God by giving him a pre-existence independent of the Father?
I wonder whether the bread and wine of the Supper are truly the body and blood of Christ, or only symbols of spiritual blessings.
I want to know whether the great Church's victory over paganism came from its organization, its dogmas, or its ability to unite the faith of the learned and the simple; which should I value most?
I am a simple believer who cannot follow the philosophic exercises of the learned; where can I find the way to the highest good that they say is hidden from people like me?
I am a Gentile Christian attracted to the ascetic life of the Jewish Christian teachers—vegetarianism, celibacy, daily washings; is this a higher path or a departure from the Gospel?
My family has kept the law of our fathers since the first believers; are we the true descendants of the earliest Christians, or have we fallen away?
I wonder whether the moral teaching of Jesus can be separated from his person, or whether the two are inseparable.
I am a teacher trying to explain the history of Christian doctrine to students; how do I avoid presenting the development as a simple unfolding of ideas?
I believe the world is God's good creation, yet I am told the present order is the work of an evil creator; how should I think of the world?
I am a Christian who has been accused of Ebionitism because I emphasize the unity of God and reject the Logos doctrine; is my faith defective?
I am tempted to think that since grace abounds, I may sin freely; how does the tradition answer this?
I am concerned that the Church has replaced the living Spirit with a class of priests and a fixed ritual; is this a corruption or a necessary development?
I want to know whether the Holy Spirit is a gift given to believers or a heavenly being distinct from the Father and the Son.
I wonder whether Paul's theology is the true foundation of Christian doctrine or only one voice among many; how should I regard him?
I am trying to understand what it means to say that Christ is the centre of the Christian religion, and whether that makes Christianity merely a religion about a person rather than about God.
I am unsure whether the good God can be angry or judge; if he is only love and mercy, what becomes of the wicked?
I am a slave and my master is a Christian; are the natural distinctions between us abolished in the Church?
I am told that the Church existed before the creation of the world and that the Christians are the true Israel; what does that make of the Jewish people?
I am told that Catholicism grew out of a compromise between Jewish and Gentile Christianity; should I accept that my church's doctrine is a mixture of two parties?
I am a teacher who wishes to prove from the prophets that Jesus' birth, death, and resurrection were foretold; is this the right use of the Old Testament?
I am attracted to the moral seriousness of the Christians I have met, but I am not sure their doctrines are true; what actually won people to this faith?
I have received a teaching about Christ from a wandering teacher, but I do not know whether it truly goes back to the Apostles; how should I judge it?
I want to know whether the Gospel can be expressed in any culture, or whether it is bound to the forms of the ancient world in which it first took shape.
I want to renounce the world and mortify the flesh, but I fear this leads me to despise God's creation; how should I practice self-control?
I am troubled that our worship uses no images and no sacrifices, while the Old Testament commanded them; how is our worship a sacrifice?
I want to join a religious community that promises blessedness, but I need a founder and a way to keep that blessedness; can a philosophy alone give me this?
I am a bishop in a small community and the prophets no longer speak as they once did; should I take over the solemn service of the word?
I am a Gentile believer who has been persuaded that the law is binding on all Christians; if I return to a law-free life, am I apostatizing?
I am married and my spouse and I wish to be received into a strict community that demands separation; must we separate to be baptized?
I am drawn to the hope of Christ's speedy return and the coming kingdom, but I also value present spiritual blessings like forgiveness and peace; how do these two hopes fit together?
I am a sinner and the righteous people of my town despise me; will Christ receive me rather than them?
I wonder whether the differences among Christians today are as serious as those in the early centuries, and what the history of dogma can teach me about them.
I am a historian writing about the early Church and I fear I am reading my own modern opinions into the past; how should I discipline myself?
